1. Moving adjacent to the black king (which is on b6 – whose adjoining squares are a5, a6, a7, b5, b7, c5, c6, and c7).

• Moving to e5: e5 is not adjacent to the black king and is not on a diagonal with the bishop. Legal.
• Moving to e6: e6 is safe from both black king and bishop. Legal.
• Moving to e7: e7 is likewise safe. Legal.

Any capture move (such as capturing the bishop on c6) isn’t allowed because c6 is adjacent to the black king.

Looking at your pieces:
• Your White King is on f4.
• Your White pawns are on a3 and g2.

Since only the king can move to escape this check and none of the pawns can block or capture the pawn on g5 in one move, you must move your king. One very attractive option is to capture the checking pawn on g5 with your king.

Analyzing the king’s possible moves:
– f4 to e3, f3, g3, e4, g4, e5, f5 are all moves that would remove the king from the checking line.
– However, capturing on g5 (move f4 to g5) eliminates the checking pawn entirely, improving your material balance.

• White’s King is on g1. Its potential moves are to an adjacent square: f1, f2, g2, h2, or h1. • The White pawn on a4 can move forward to a5.

• The White pawn on c5 cannot move forward to c6 because that square is occupied by Black’s bishop on c6, and there’s no immediate capture possibility on the diagonals (b6 or d6 are empty).

• The White pawn on h3 can advance to h4.

After a brief look at the safety of the king’s potential squares, moving Kg1–f2 looks attractive: f2 isn’t exposed to any immediate threats. The board shows a white king on h4, a white pawn on h3, and a black king on f3. White’s pawn on h3 cannot move forward because the white king occupies h4, and there isn’t an enemy piece diagonally available to capture. That leaves the white king as the only piece with legal moves. The white king at h4 can normally move one square in any direction. Its neighbor squares are g3, g4, g5, h3, and h5. However, the rules of chess forbid kings from moving into squares adjacent to the opposing king. Since the black king is on f3, the white king’s moves to g3 and g4 would bring it adjacent to the black king and are illegal. Also, h3 is occupied by the white pawn leaving only g5 and h5 as legal moves.

After evaluating these options, I choose to move the white king from h4 to h5.

make_move h4h5

Player_White (to Proxy):

It looks like our current board is represented by the FEN "8/8/2k5/8/2K5/8/1P4PP/8 w - - 3 64". On the board, White’s pieces are the king on c4 and pawns on b2, g2, and h2, while Black only has a king on c6. Since there isn’t any piece on e2, the move e2e4 is illegal.

Reviewing the legal moves, one reasonable plan is to use the king actively in this king and pawn endgame. A nice idea is to move the king closer to the enemy king while keeping it centralized. For example, moving the white king from c4 to d4 (UCI: c4d4) “shoulder off” the black king and help support the advancement of our pawns.

make_move c4d4

White’s pawns (on g2 and h2) can move forward (and optionally two squares from their starting positions) but no captures are available since no enemy piece lies diagonally ahead.

Based on the board setup, I notice that White’s only pieces are the king on d8 and two pawns on g2 and h2. Meanwhile, Black has a king on c6 and three pawns on a7, a5, and h4. Since it’s White’s turn, one strategy in an endgame with few pieces is to improve the king’s activity. White’s king on d8 can move to one of the following adjacent squares, but it must avoid squares immediately adjacent to Black’s king on c6. In particular, from d8, the adjacent squares are:
 • c8 (legal; not adjacent to Black’s king, because the king would be two squares vertically from c6)
 • c7 (illegal since c7 is directly above c6, making the kings adjacent)
 • d7 (illegal for the same reason: from d7, the king would be diagonally adjacent to Black’s king on c6)
 • e7 (legal; it brings the king nearer to the center without violating the proximity rule)
 • e8 (legal)

Among these, King move d8 to e7 seems appealing because it centralizes the king without stepping too close to Black’s king. Alternatively, one could consider advancing one of the pawns to develop an advantage, but king centralization is often crucial in such minimalist endgames.

I’ll choose to move the White king from d8 to e7.

make_move d8e7

Based on the current board, our white pieces are as follows:

• White King (♔) is on g5.
• White Pawn (♙) is on a2.

Black’s pieces include:
• Black King (♚) on d5.
• Black Pawn (♟) on a5.
• Black Queen (♛) on h2.

Looking at the king on g5, its potential one‐square moves (provided they keep the king out of check) are:
 – Moving to f5, f6, g4, or g6 are all candidates.
It is important to note that moves leading the king onto the h‐file (h4, h5, or h6) are not legal because they would be exposed to a direct check along the vertical file by the black queen on h2. Similarly, the square f4 is ruled out as it lies on the diagonal h2→g3→f4.

Reviewing our options, one plan is to improve the king’s position while avoiding any precarious alignment with the black queen. Moving the king from g5 to f5 seems like a healthy, safe, and centralizing move. It avoids harmful lines from the queen and continues development—an important principle even in adverse material situations. (Our pawn on a2 remains an option too—advancing to a3 or a4—but with only these two pieces it is critical to improve the king’s activity and hope for a drawing fortress or a perpetual check scenario, given black's material advantage.)

Thus, I choose to move the White King from g5 to f5.

make_move g5f5

As White, you have two pieces: your king on a3 and a pawn on a2. The pawn on a2 can only move one step forward (to a3) but that square is occupied by your king, and it cannot move two steps because a3 is blocked. Thus your only legal moves are king moves.

From a3, your king’s potential moves are:
• a2 – but that square is occupied by your pawn.
• a4 – however, note that moving to a4 makes it directly adjacent to Black’s king (♚ on b5, whose adjacent squares include a4), which is illegal.
• b2 – legal.
• b3 – legal.
• b4 – illegal (adjacent to b5).

Between b2 and b3, the move to b3 places your king more actively in the center and closer to the Black king, potentially aiding in any endgame plan with your extra pawn. Therefore, the move King from a3 to b3 (UCI move: a3b3) is a strong choice.

• King moves:
 – The white king on g1 can move to f1, f2, or h1 (note that g2 and h2 are occupied by white pawns).
